sweep_summary: The stress-title sweep for Mende (mend1266, catalog 'tonal', deciding source Dwyer 1978 'What sort of tone language is Mende?' SAL 9(2)) turned up one item: Dwyer 1978 'Idiosyncratic, suprasegmental processes in Mende', SAL 9(3):333-343 (Glottolog's 331-391 pagination is wrong). I fetched sources the open full-issue PDF from journals.flvc.org, text, logged) and read the article (PDF pp. 95-105). It is a tone-only autosegmental study (high-falling tone pattern from apocope/syncope, demorphologized compounds, tonal/segmental parity, the definite suffix -i) and contains no statement about word stress or accent placement; a grep for stress/accent/prominence terms over the article returns nothing. It confirms the 'tonal' coding and does not supersede the catalog's deciding source. Nothing remains to acquire from this sweep (priority none); the earlier audit's wishlist (Innes 1962/1971, Aginsky 1935, Conteh et al. 1983, Toda 1989) is unchanged.

new_statements.quote: In my paper read before the conference on African linguistics in Gainesville [Dwyer 1976], I claimed that Mende was not a suprasegmental tone language of the type envisioned by Leben [1973]. Yet, in that paper I suggested that there were a number of processes in Mende which nevertheless appeared to be of a suprasegmental nature. ... Mende contains a small set of disyllabic morphemes that display a high-falling tone pattern. ... Because examples of this tonal pattern are few in number and because this pattern is not present in Proto Southwestern Mande, the high-falling tone pattern appears to be a fairly recent development in Mende.
new_statements.citation: Dwyer, David J. 1978. "Idiosyncratic, suprasegmental processes in Mende." Studies in African Linguistics 9(3):333-343.
new_statements.reading: A specialist tonology paper that describes Mende word prosody entirely in terms of lexical tone melodies (H HL, L H L) associated to syllables, with no word-stress or accent statement anywhere. It confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding but adds nothing on stress; it is the companion to, not a replacement for, the catalog's deciding source (Dwyer 1978, SAL 9(2), which addresses the type of tone language directly).

[Glottolog ref 56791 gives pages 331-391; the issue table of contents and running page numbers give 333-343.]
sources.quote: p.333: "In my paper read before the conference on African linguistics in Gainesville [Dwyer 1976], I claimed that Mende was not a suprasegmental tone language of the type envisioned by Leben [1973]. Yet, in that paper I suggested that there were a number of processes in Mende which nevertheless appeared to be of a suprasegmental nature." ... "Mende contains a small set of disyllabic morphemes that display a high-falling tone pattern. These words, taken from Spears [1968] are given in (1): ngɔngɔ tooth, hokpo navel, poko imitate, tokpla seat, bottom, mbembe circle." p.343: "I have examined a number of idiosyncratic phonological (suprasegmental) processes ... the interrelationship between various melodic tiers such as tone, vowel quality, etc."
sources.locator: sec. 1 Introduction and sec. 2, printed p. 333 (PDF p. 95); sec. 5 Conclusion, printed p. 343 (PDF p. 105)
sources.note: Nothing. The article is a tone-only study (the sequel to the catalog's deciding source, Dwyer 1978 'What sort of tone language is Mende?', SAL 9(2)): it treats the rise of the high-falling (H HL) tone pattern via apocope/syncope, 'demorphologized' compounds with an L H L melody, a 'principle of tonal/segmental parity', and the definite suffix -i, all in an autosegmental framework. sources.citation: Spears, Richard A. 1967. Basic Course in Mende. Evanston: Northwestern University (US Office of Education report BR-6-1491-2; ERIC ED012018), 579 pp. scanned of ERIC microfiche, archive.org micro_IA41153663_0429.
sources.quote: 'It can be said that words like kal.i 'hoe' and kal.i 'snake' are alike except for tone and meaning. The tone is part of each word and tonal information for each word must be learned as part of the word. ... A word can change its tones according to the tones of the words near it or grammatical structures it occurs in.' No statement on word stress/accent anywhere in the 579 pp (grep stress/accent/prominence: only 'seamstress', 'mistress', and 'grave accent' as a tone diacritic).
sources.locator: Introduction (scanned lines 340-341: 'Tone and morphophonemics are considered to be of such major importance that the entire course is built around these two areas'); Chapter Two 'Tone', printed p.177 (scanned lines 16897-16905)
